title: BFCM 2026: Who’s Already in Your Inbox?
summary: See who sent the first Black Friday emails of 2026, the early plays brands are running, and whether going early pays off. Take the quiz.
body_markdown:
Black Friday falls on November 27 and Cyber Monday on November 30. That's days away, not months.


If you run email, your BFCM plan has probably been locked since August. Most brands start planning in late July and finalize by mid-August ([Modash](https://www.modash.io/blog/black-friday-prep-campaigns) ). The hard part is behind you. Now comes the fun part: seeing what everyone actually sends.


## What we're seeing so far


Air Canada sent a "Black Friday in July" email in, yes, July. Big-box retailers have run "early Black Friday" events since late October, and a handful of brands have opened members-only early access.


But most brands haven't sent a single Black Friday email yet. For now, Christmas and other seasonal sales are winning the inbox.


## Test yourself: when did Black Friday start?


Pick an answer to see how early the first sends landed.


Quick quiz


#### When did the first "Black Friday" email of 2026 land?


**A, July 9. Yes, really.** Air Canada sent "Black Friday in July" 141 days before the real thing, teasing up to 40% off vacation packages for two weeks only. Most marketers hadn't even finalized their own BFCM plans.


If you guessed otherwise, you weren't far off:


- **B) September 19** is when a home-decor retailer ran the earliest Black Friday ad[RivalSweeper](https://www.rivalsweeper.com/research/black-friday-2026-rival-watch) tracked in 2025: a Facebook and Instagram sign-up ad, 70 days out. Wrong year, and an ad, not an email.
- **C) October 15** brought this season's first Black Friday email in[RivalSweeper's tracking](https://www.rivalsweeper.com/research/black-friday-2026-rival-watch) : a beauty brand's "Cyber Monday leak," 40% off, sent almost to the day as last year.
- **D) November 1** is when H&M started calling its emails "Early Black Friday." Early Black Friday is its own marketing moment now.


Bonus round


#### In the first week of November, which phrase showed up in more marketing emails?


**Christmas, 7 to 5,** across 122 tracked emails ([RivalSweeper](https://www.rivalsweeper.com/research/black-friday-2026-rival-watch) , Oct 30 to Nov 5). Santa is ahead on points.

Source:[RivalSweeper](https://www.rivalsweeper.com/research/black-friday-2026-rival-watch) , Black Friday 2026 Rival Watch; Air Canada email, July 9, 2026


### Christmas is winning the inbox


Marketing emails tracked Oct 30 to Nov 5, 2026 (122 total). Source: RivalSweeper


## From our inboxes


We've been screenshotting everything. Here's what has landed so far.


### Air Canada, July 9: "Black Friday in July"


Sent in high summer, 141 days early, with up to 40% off select Air Canada Vacations packages if booked by July 19. The preheader simply read "2 weeks only." It's Christmas in July with a fresh coat of paint.


**The play: borrow the name.** To shoppers, "Black Friday" now means "the big sale," not a date on the calendar. Anyone can host one, in any month.


### H&M, November 1: "15% off $100 or 25% off $125"


Notice what's missing from the subject line? Black Friday. The phrase only shows up in the preheader and a small label above the offer. Two spend tiers, free shipping, a 48-hour window online, and 30% off select styles in store for the week.


### H&M: "New Traditions"


In this one, Black Friday shrinks to a ticker. The hero of this one is pure Christmas: kids in tinsel, festive plaid and "a sprinkle of sequins for the season ahead." The only Black Friday mention is a thin black bar up top: 30% off select styles, in store only. Right under the logo, a personal line tells you exactly how many points you are from your next member reward.


**The play: let Christmas lead.** Christmas sets the mood, Black Friday adds the urgency. One email does both, and the brand never has to pick a season.

## Is earlier actually better?


Not really. The best deals, content and campaigns still beat getting there first.


Last year's earliest Black Friday advertiser went live 70 days out. This year, that same brand waited until 36 days out. Most brands still start late: in 2025, the typical first Black Friday ad ran just 11 days before the day itself ([RivalSweeper](https://www.rivalsweeper.com/research/black-friday-2026-rival-watch) ).


### How far ahead did the first Black Friday ad run?


Days before Black Friday. Source: RivalSweeper, Black Friday 2026 Rival Watch


Going early Waiting


**Shoppers are already buying.** 71% plan to start before Black Friday, and 46% before November (Attentive). **Discounts stay special.** Only 32% expect deals in early November, so an early discount can teach people to hold out for more.


**Quieter inboxes.** November 2025 email volume rose 32% year over year, with the sharpest jump the week before Cyber Week (Sinch Mailjet). **Fewer sends overall.** Unsubscribes rose 42% year over year around Black Friday 2025 ([Ometria](https://ometria.com/blog/black-friday-2025-data) ), so every extra email has a cost.


**A bigger list.** You grow the list you'll mail on the big day. **Better margins.** You protect margin for the days that convert.


One number worth taping to your monitor: in[Ometria's BFCM 2025 data](https://ometria.com/blog/black-friday-2025-data) , automated emails made up 2% of sends and drove 28% of revenue. Small but mighty.

## What to do next


- **Start a swipe file.** Screenshot every early send, with its date. It's ready-made inspiration for next year's planning deck.
- **Keep a fast lane for changes.** Dates move, offers get extended, and a competitor will undercut you on a random Tuesday. The win now is same-day edits, not new templates. In Dyspatch, you brief your agent in plain language and get back a finished, on-brand email, with brand guardrails and localization built in. It's how Canva ships 20+ emails a week, and how[Homebase cut email production by 80%](https://www.dyspatch.io/blog/how-homebase-cut-email-production-by-80-percent/) .
- **Watch, don't copy.** First movers repeat their own playbook every year. Their timing tells you more about them than about your customers.
